PHASE 3 · ADVANCED HEALTH ASSESSMENT & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS

Week 46 — Lesson 70: Eye, ENT & Oral Assessment

FNP-level goal: Evaluate vision change, red eye, ocular trauma, ear pain/hearing change, nasal symptoms, sore throat, oral lesions, and neck complaints through function, airway/vision protection, focused examination, and safe disposition. Recognize when a seemingly minor eye, ear, or throat complaint may represent a sight-, hearing-, airway-, neurologic-, or systemic-threatening condition.

Learning Objectives

  • Identify emergency red flags in visual loss, red eye, ocular trauma, hearing change, and throat/oral complaints.
  • Perform and document a focused eye, ear, nose, mouth, and neck examination within training and equipment limits.
  • Use symptom pattern, laterality, timing, exposures, and host risk to build a differential.
  • Distinguish common outpatient syndromes from conditions needing emergency or expedited specialty care.
  • Use targeted visual acuity, otoscopy, hearing assessment, swabs, imaging, and referral to answer a clinical question.
  • Provide clear return precautions and closed-loop follow-up.

Part 1 — Protect Vision, Airway, and Neurologic Function First

Start with acuity and stability. For eye complaints, ask about sudden vision change, severe pain, photophobia, headache/nausea, contact-lens use, trauma, chemical exposure, discharge, flashes/floaters, curtain/shadow, diplopia, and immunocompromise. Measure visual acuity in each eye when feasible before topical treatment. New severe or painless monocular visual loss, field loss, a curtain/shadow, painful red eye with photophobia or reduced vision, penetrating/chemical injury, proptosis, restricted painful eye movement, or trauma with suspected globe/orbital injury requires urgent emergency/ophthalmology pathway assessment.

For throat/oral complaints, assess voice, work of breathing, stridor, drooling, ability to swallow secretions, hydration, trismus, neck swelling, fever, toxicity, immune compromise, and rapid progression. Airway symptoms outrank a detailed outpatient oral examination. Do not repeatedly manipulate the oropharynx of a patient with suspected impending airway compromise; arrange emergency care according to local protocol.

Part 2 — Build the Eye, ENT, and Oral Problem Representation

Define the time course: sudden versus gradual, unilateral versus bilateral, constant versus episodic, recurrent versus first event. Determine whether the main issue is pain, vision loss, redness, itching, discharge, hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, congestion, swallowing pain, oral pain, neck mass, or hoarseness. Ask about recent URI/allergy symptoms, fever, sick contacts, water exposure, trauma/foreign body, barotrauma, loud noise, dental disease, smoking/vaping, reflux, sexual history when relevant, travel, immune suppression, diabetes, anticoagulants, and medication changes.

Laterality and function matter. Bilateral itchy eyes with watery discharge create a different differential than one painful photophobic red eye. Gradual bilateral age-related hearing change differs from sudden unilateral loss with tinnitus or dizziness. A simple sore throat with cough/rhinorrhea differs from rapidly worsening throat pain with muffled voice, drooling, trismus, or neck swelling.

Part 3 — Focused Eye Examination

Document visual acuity, pupils and any asymmetry, gross visual fields when appropriate, extraocular movements, eyelid and periorbital findings, conjunctival injection/discharge, corneal clarity, photophobia, and whether pain occurs with eye movement. Observe for contact lenses, foreign body, trauma, hyphema, irregular pupil, proptosis, chemosis, or inability to open the eye. Compare both eyes and document the baseline if known.

Do not use a reassuring conjunctivitis label when visual acuity is reduced, pain is substantial, photophobia is present, corneal abnormality is suspected, contact-lens risk exists, or there is trauma/chemical exposure. Fluorescein examination, tonometry, slit lamp assessment, dilated retinal examination, and ocular imaging depend on training, available equipment, and local protocol. If a sight-threatening process is plausible, referral/transfer is more important than completing every office test.

Part 4 — Red Eye: Not Every Red Eye Is Conjunctivitis

Itching, watery discharge, bilateral involvement, and preserved vision can support an allergic or viral pattern, but the FNP must screen for pain, photophobia, vision change, contact lenses, trauma, corneal opacity, ciliary flush, pupil abnormalities, severe headache/nausea, and unilateral severe findings. Painful red eye with reduced acuity or photophobia can reflect keratitis, uveitis, scleritis, acute pressure-related disease, or other urgent pathology.

Contact-lens wear with pain/redness is a higher-risk context for corneal disease. Avoid reflex topical steroid treatment or delayed referral in uncertain painful red eye. Document the lens history, remove lenses when clinically appropriate, and escalate based on local ophthalmology/emergency pathways.

Part 5 — Acute Vision Change, Flashes, Floaters, and Field Defect

Sudden painless monocular visual loss is an emergency until appropriately evaluated. New flashes with a shower of floaters, a peripheral shadow, or a gray curtain can signal retinal tear/detachment and needs urgent ophthalmic assessment. Transient monocular visual loss can be vascular and requires urgent evaluation; do not assume it is merely ocular migraine without considering the complete neurologic and vascular context.

Differentiate monocular from binocular symptoms, positive visual phenomena from loss of vision, and gradual refractive change from abrupt field loss. Ask about trauma, severe myopia, prior eye surgery, vascular risk, headache/scalp tenderness/jaw symptoms in the appropriate patient, and neurologic deficits. New visual symptoms with face/arm weakness, speech difficulty, ataxia, or altered mental status should trigger an acute stroke pathway.

Part 6 — Ocular Trauma and Chemical Exposure

Ask what entered or struck the eye, when it occurred, whether high-velocity metal/glass was involved, and whether there is pain, visual change, photophobia, double vision, bleeding, or foreign-body sensation. A suspected open globe, penetrating injury, severe blunt trauma, hyphema, irregular pupil, marked vision loss, or orbital signs needs emergency care. Avoid pressure on a potentially injured globe.

Chemical injury requires immediate irrigation and emergency ophthalmic assessment according to local protocol; do not delay for a complete history, visual testing, or paperwork. Record the agent if known without sacrificing time to obtain it. The FNP role is rapid decontamination/escalation and safe transfer, not a prolonged office workup of a potentially vision-threatening exposure.

Part 7 — Ear Pain, Otoscopy, and Hearing Change

Ask about pain, drainage, fever, recent URI/allergy, water exposure, trauma, foreign body, hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, facial weakness, diabetes/immune compromise, mastoid tenderness, and severe headache. Examine the external ear, canal, tympanic membrane when visualization is safe, surrounding skin, mastoid, cranial findings when relevant, and hearing function. Do not insert objects into the canal or irrigate when tympanic membrane status, foreign body type, perforation, or procedural safety is uncertain.

Sudden hearing loss—often unilateral, sometimes with tinnitus, fullness, or dizziness—needs prompt evaluation and audiometric pathway access. It should not be automatically attributed to wax, congestion, or “an ear infection” without appropriate examination. Severe otalgia with systemic illness, mastoid/postauricular swelling, cranial deficits, immunocompromise, or diabetes requires urgent escalation for complicated infection and other causes.

Part 8 — Nasal, Sinus, Throat, and Neck Assessment

For nasal/sinus symptoms, establish duration, severity, fever, facial swelling, eye symptoms, neurologic symptoms, dental pain, discharge, trauma, epistaxis, and immune risk. Eye swelling, pain with eye movement, vision change, severe headache, altered mental status, or rapidly progressive facial swelling changes the urgency. Avoid a routine “sinusitis” label when orbital, dental, neurologic, or systemic disease is possible.

For sore throat, examine hydration, voice, oral cavity, tonsils when safe, uvula, neck motion, lymph nodes, rash, respiratory effort, and hydration. Cough/rhinorrhea/hoarseness can support viral illness but do not override airway signs. Difficulty breathing or swallowing, drooling, blood in saliva, dehydration, progressive neck swelling, muffled voice, trismus, or toxicity needs urgent assessment. Swab testing should follow the clinical question and current local guidelines, not replace an airway evaluation.

Part 9 — Oral Lesions, Dental Disease, and Head/Neck Cancer Safety

Describe oral ulcers, plaques, vesicles, pigment, bleeding, dental caries, gingival swelling, fluctuance, trauma, and duration. Ask about pain, fever, dysphagia, weight loss, tobacco/vape and alcohol exposure, immunosuppression, sexual exposure when relevant, denture fit, xerostomia, and prior lesions. A dental infection can spread beyond a tooth; facial swelling, trismus, dysphagia, floor-of-mouth elevation, systemic symptoms, or airway concern requires urgent escalation.

Persistent, unexplained oral ulceration, leukoplakic/erythroplakic change, unexplained neck mass, recurrent bleeding, weight loss, persistent voice change, or progressive swallowing symptoms requires an appropriate dental/ENT/oral-medicine/oncology pathway. Do not repeatedly treat a persistent lesion as thrush or trauma without reassessing the diagnosis and arranging follow-up.

Part 10 — Tests and Referrals: Answer a Question

Visual acuity is a key functional test for most eye complaints. Otoscopy and basic hearing screening can refine a hearing complaint, but formal audiometry may be needed for sudden or unclear loss. Rapid strep or other throat tests, cultures, microscopy, pregnancy testing, glucose, imaging, and specialty studies should answer a specific question. Routine imaging is not a replacement for escalation in a sight-, airway-, or neurologic-threatening presentation.

Photographs and teleconsultation can help only through approved secure systems and with consent, especially for eye, oral, and facial findings. Document laterality, onset, acuity/function, examination limits, treatment given, referral destination, and exact precautions. Ensure a pending result or referral has a named owner; a “refer to ENT/ophthalmology” plan is unsafe if the patient cannot access care or does not understand when to go to the emergency department instead.

Part 11 — Clinical Case: Painful Red Eye

A contact-lens wearer has unilateral red eye, pain, photophobia, and reduced visual acuity. There is little discharge.

FNP reasoning: do not label this routine conjunctivitis. Contact-lens exposure plus pain, photophobia, and reduced vision raises concern for corneal disease or another urgent eye condition. Arrange same-day urgent ophthalmic/emergency assessment according to local pathway.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: Flashes and a Curtain

A 61-year-old notices new flashes, numerous floaters, and a dark curtain spreading across one eye. There is no pain.

FNP reasoning: painless does not mean low risk. This symptom pattern can suggest retinal tear/detachment and requires urgent ophthalmic assessment. Do not wait for a routine optometry appointment.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: Sore Throat With Airway Risk

A patient presents with rapidly worsening throat pain, fever, muffled voice, drooling, difficulty swallowing, and visible neck swelling.

FNP reasoning: this is an airway and deep-neck-infection concern, not a routine pharyngitis visit. Keep the patient safe, avoid provocative examination, and arrange emergency evaluation.

FNP Eye, ENT & Oral Framework

  1. Protect function first: vision, airway, neurologic status, hearing, hydration, and hemodynamics.
  2. Define the symptom: laterality, onset, vision/hearing function, pain, photophobia, discharge, trauma/exposure, and associated systemic findings.
  3. Examine within scope: acuity, pupils, movements, external eye; external ear/canal/TM; nose, mouth, throat, and neck when safe.
  4. Identify red flags: visual loss/field defect, painful photophobic red eye, trauma/chemical exposure, sudden hearing loss, mastoid/cranial findings, and airway/neck compromise.
  5. Test with a question: acuity, otoscopy/audiometry, targeted swabs/labs, imaging, or emergency/specialty pathway.
  6. Do not anchor: “conjunctivitis,” “wax,” “sinus infection,” or “strep throat” cannot explain away function loss or danger signs.
  7. Close the loop: document function and laterality, give exact return precautions, and confirm referral/result ownership.

High-Yield Summary

Eye complaints: document visual acuity; painful red eye with photophobia/reduced vision, acute vision loss, curtain/field defect, trauma, or chemical exposure needs urgent escalation.
Flashes/floaters: new shower of floaters, flashes, shadow, or curtain can indicate retinal tear/detachment.
Sudden hearing change: needs prompt evaluation rather than automatic attribution to congestion or wax.
Throat/oral symptoms: breathing/swallowing difficulty, drooling, muffled voice, trismus, neck swelling, toxicity, or dehydration demands urgent assessment.
Oral lesions: persistent, bleeding, nonhealing, unexplained, or high-risk lesions need appropriate referral.
FNP standard: integrate function, laterality, onset, focused exam, testing purpose, specialty access, and explicit emergency precautions.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Eye, ENT, oral, dental, airway, trauma, imaging, treatment, referral, and emergency-disposition decisions must follow current evidence, local protocols, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
